I've worked this land in Quzhou for over forty years. At my age I'm not going to experiment. The North China Plain soil here, the local grain buyers, the input supply network — everything is built around wheat and maize. I plant winter wheat in October, harvest in June, then immediately follow with summer maize. That's what I'll do this year.

My land is about 8 mu. All of it goes into the rotation — no piece sits idle.

For wheat I'll use an improved variety from the county seed station. The Jimai line has held up well against powdery mildew, which has been worse in recent years. I've cut my nitrogen back from what I used to apply — I've read the research and I know over-fertilizing just runs off into the groundwater and costs me money I don't need to spend. I'll put down base fertilizer before planting and top-dress once at jointing. Three irrigations: one at sowing because the soil will be dry in October, one at the wintering stage to help root establishment, and one at jointing. If it's dry at grain fill I'll do a fourth but I try to avoid that.

For maize I use hybrid seed — Zhengdan 958 or whatever the station is pushing this season. Hybrids are worth the price. I direct-seed into the wheat stubble. No-till saves my back and keeps moisture in the soil. Summer rains carry most of the water need so I only plan one irrigation, maybe two if July is short on rain.

Pesticides: wheat gets a herbicide spray in early spring and one fungicide if I see disease. Maize gets one herbicide pass post-emergence and I stay alert for fall armyworm — I'll spray if I find it.
